extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and general readers interested in public finance and taxation policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and design principles for taxation systems (customs, excise, duties) — i.e., what makes a good, effective, equitable tax system and its administration. The guidance addresses rate-setting, tax base, incidence, administration, and practical remedies for evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, perspicuity, precision, and distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax laws and rates should be expressed with perspicuity, precision, and distinctness so as to avoid uncertainty about classification and liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book of rates for customs is criticised as exceedingly comprehensive and often uncertain about how to class particular goods, causing ruin or vexation. By contrast, duties of excise are praised for their greater perspicuity and precision. Anti-pattern: highly detailed, ambiguous enumerations that leave officers and importers unsure which article applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of the tax base (confine to few general goods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confine duties to a few articles of the most general use and consumption to simplify administration and make contribution proportionate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues duties of excise are imposed on a few widely consumed articles and suggests customs could similarly be limited (e.g., wines, sugars, tea). If extended to almost all goods, public warehouses and administration become impractical. Example: restricting customs to a few general-use imports could make customs as simple and certain as excise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality / equity of contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should make the greater part of society contribute to public revenue in proportion to their respective expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excise revenue is supposed to fall as equally upon contributors as customs. The principle is that taxation should be proportional to expense; the consumer’s voluntary purchases influence who pays. Relates to Adam Smith’s maxim that subjects should pay in proportion to their abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes as instrument of revenue, not monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should be employed as instruments of revenue and never for creating monopolies or to give domestic merchants unfair protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many foreign-manufacture taxes were historically imposed not for revenue but for monopoly/protection. The recommendation: remove prohibitions, subject foreign manufactures to moderate taxes chosen to maximize revenue rather than to monopolize the home market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid setting rates that reduce consumption or encourage smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: High tax rates that diminish consumption or create strong incentives to smuggle can produce lower net revenue than more moderate rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two adverse effects of high taxes are (1) reduced consumption (remedied by lowering the tax) and (2) encouragement of smuggling (remedied by lowering tax or strengthening administration). Example: heavy duties often produce less revenue than moderate taxes because of decreased consumption and smugglers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative design to prevent evasion (increase difficulty of smuggling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design administration systems (inspections, warehouses, excise-like procedures) that increase the difficulty and reduce the temptation to smuggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excise administration is credited with obstructing smugglers more effectively than customs. Proposals include allowing importers to store in private or public warehouses under custom-house officer supervision, duties paid on release for home consumption, and public warehouses for exports to be duty-free. Anti-pattern: lax administration that makes smuggling easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow deferment/choice of warehousing to reduce burden and smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide options (private warehouse with inspection or public bonded warehouses) so duties need not be advanced at importation and can be paid on removal for consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If merchants may lodge goods in bonded warehouses and pay duties only when released for home consumption (exports duty-free with security), importers avoid advancing taxes and can sell more cheaply. Caveat: if duties apply to almost all goods, public warehouses may be impracticable, and delicate goods may not be safe in public storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of assessment and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should be perfectly certain or assessed so as to leave no doubt concerning either what ought to be paid or when it ought to be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certainty reduces disputes and administrative burden. Uncertainty in customs arises not from the nature of customs but from inaccurately or unskilfully expressed laws. Certainty is one of the core maxims of good taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience in time and mode of payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should be imposed and collected at a time and in a mode that is convenient for contributors—ideally payable piece‑meal as consumption occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on luxuries can normally be paid piece‑meal in proportion to purchases, making them among the most convenient taxes. Example: excise duties payable as the commodity is bought rather than as a lump advance by importers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate tax base measurement (value vs bulk/weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose duties according to the base that best matches the purpose: bulk/weight for local maintenance (peages/turnpikes), value for proportional taxation; avoid using value-based transit duties that function like inland customs and obstruct internal commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage duties originally for road/navigation maintenance are properly based on bulk or weight. When such duties are assessed by supposed value, they become inland customs/excise and greatly obstruct interior commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target luxuries, not necessary expenses of the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should, where possible, be placed on luxuries rather than on necessities of the inferior ranks of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states explicitly: 'it is the luxuries, and not the necessary expense of the inferior ranks of people, that ought ever to be taxed.' Taxing necessities would ultimately harm the fund that pays all taxes (annual produce) and distort wages/demand for labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exemptions that create unequal burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not grant exemptions or privileges (e.g., exempting private brewing/distilling) that impose a heavier relative burden on the poor and produce unjust inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemption for private brewing/distilling benefits the rich who brew privately, making taxes fall lighter on the rich than the poor. The author calls such exemptions 'most unjust and unequal' and recommends their removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess incidence carefully (who ultimately pays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the final payment of a tax falls upon consumer, producer, landlord (rent), or some other group; monopoly prices and market structure affect incidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: malt/beer duties have historically been passed on to consumers rather than reducing producers’ profits. Monopoly-priced goods (e.g., certain wines, sugar under monopoly pricing) may shift the burden differently—taxing monopolist gains is often appropriate because those gains can be reached by taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider total revenue effects, including evasion and administrative feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When redesigning taxes (e.g., raising malt tax but lowering distillery duties), consider how changes affect smuggling incentives, opportunities for fraud, and the net revenue—moderate single taxes can sometimes raise more revenue than multiple heavier taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical arithmetic on malt/distillery taxes suggests trebling the malt tax (and reducing distillery duties) might produce more revenue than the current complex set of duties, because it reduces opportunities and temptations to defraud. Administrative realities (bulk, value, perishability) shape what is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match administrative arrangements to the nature of goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Design storage, inspection, and inspection-frequency rules consistent with the physical characteristics and preservation needs of goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public warehouses may be impracticable for a wide range of goods or for delicate goods requiring careful preservation; some commodities can safely be kept in public bonded warehouses (e.g., rum/excise examples), others cannot. Anti-pattern: one-size-fits-all warehousing that damages delicate imports or is logistically infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to adjust duties dynamically to maximize revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the level of duties occasionally (heighten or lower) according to what is most likely to afford the greatest revenue, using taxation as an instrument of revenue rather than monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests duties should be 'occasionally either heightened or lowered' to maximize revenue. This implies continuous monitoring of consumption, smuggling, and market responses rather than rigid adherence to fixed nominal rates.
